episode_title: 481 Do Roth Conversions Make Sense in 2026?
question: What is the golden window for Roth conversions and when does it occur in retirement?
transcript_excerpt: The golden window is the ideal time between retirement and when required minimum distributions start. If you're born after 1960, RMDs start at age 73; if born after 1960 (correction: should be a later birth year for age 75), it starts at age 75. This is typically when your tax rate is lower because you're not earning as much, making it the ideal time to pursue conversions.

episode_title: 481 Do Roth Conversions Make Sense in 2026?
question: How does tax rate arbitrage work in Roth conversion planning?
transcript_excerpt: Tax rate arbitrage means taking advantage of a lower current tax bracket to convert money before being pushed into a higher bracket by required minimum distributions. For example, if someone is in the 12% tax bracket now but will jump to 22% when RMDs start, you fill up the 12% bracket by converting, paying taxes at the lower rate now instead of the higher rate later.

episode_title: 481 Do Roth Conversions Make Sense in 2026?
question: What are the main tax advantages of converting to a Roth account?
transcript_excerpt: Money in a Roth account grows tax-free for the rest of your life and is not subject to required minimum distributions for beneficiaries, who can distribute it over 10 years without paying tax. The appreciation that happens in the Roth account avoids future taxes, unlike tax-deferred accounts where every distribution dollar is taxable.

episode_title: 481 Do Roth Conversions Make Sense in 2026?
question: How does Social Security taxation factor into Roth conversion decisions?
transcript_excerpt: Whether a Roth conversion causes your Social Security to become more taxable depends on provisional income rules. Not every dollar from Social Security is necessarily taxable—it depends on all your income sources. A conversion can increase taxable income and cause more of your Social Security benefits to become subject to taxation.

episode_title: 481 Do Roth Conversions Make Sense in 2026?
question: What is the apple orchard analogy for understanding Roth versus traditional tax-deferred accounts?
transcript_excerpt: With a Roth, you pay tax on the seed (initial contribution) but never again. With traditional tax-deferred accounts, you don't pay taxes on the seed, but every apple you pull off the tree (every distribution) for the rest of your life is taxable. Most people prefer paying taxes on the seed upfront rather than on the ongoing harvest.
